newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr needs support after offshore sales.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr needs support after offshore sales.

text.p: The Australian dollar slunk lower at the midsession after selling from U.S. and Japanese names stripped a 1/3 cent off it.

Traders said the currency found good support from exporters and Asian investors around US$0.7730 and there was talk of more bids down to last week's base at US$0.7720. If this held, it would likely see a brisk short covering rally back to US$0.7765, a scenario which had become all too familiar recently.
A dwindling interest rate advantage meant there was a greater risk of a break lower, however, in which case a test of a long-term bear target at US$0.7680 was likely.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar was holding its own at US$0.7740/45 after edging up from a US$0.7734 low but was still off its early US$0.7760/65 and Thursday's late US$0.7756/61.

There was some action on the crosses where the U.S. dollar was making waves after the weekend G7 meeting ended with no explicit plan to counter the strength of the currency. Various officials said the U.S. had agreed with Japan that a further rise in the dollar was not appropriate and currencies should not move out of line with their fundamentals.
Dealers, however, felt the fundamentals fully supported a firmer U.S. dollar and chased it higher in response.
The dollar was up at 1.7342/47 marks and 126.84/89 yen from 1.7270/80 and 126.20/30 late in New York Friday.

The local currency followed against the mark to reach 1.3447/61 from 1.3323/37 late here Thursday, but ran into a sizeable sell order on the yen -- rumoured to be around A$100 million -- which held it back at 98.10/20 from 98.00/10.
Chief amongst the reasons for the U.S. dollar's strength were expectations the Federal Reserve would respond to above trend growth by hiking rates again at its May 20 meeting.
In contrast the risk in Australia was that disappointing employment growth would prompt the Reserve Bank to ease again.

Favourable consumer price data and a benign living wage decision last week appeared to have provided some scope for a rate cut. Weekly earnings figures this Thursday may, or may not, add to that with forecasts differing widely on the likely rise.

Median forecasts see annual growth accelerating to 4.3 percent from 3.9 in Q4, but estimates range from 4.0 to 4.6 percent. The latter would take earnings growth into the RBA's danger zone of 4.5-5.0 percent and would be viewed as lessening the chance of a cut.
Analysts were more confident that data due on the real side of the economy would show activity picked up in Q1.

Building approvals on Thursday should confirm the ongoing recovery in the housing market with a 2.0 percent rise expected for March and talk it could be as high as 15 percent due to one-off developments such as the Olympic village.
Retail trade for March, on Friday, was seen flat after strong gains the previous two months which would still lift real trade by a healthy 2.4 percent in the quarter.
Such a gain would add around 0.5-0.6 point to GDP growth in the March quarter and reinforce most analysts' belief another official easing would be pro-cyclical and therefore was not needed.
The RBA's view would be clearer after its monthly meeting on May 6 since analysts reasoned that if it was minded to move it would do so on May 7.
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane would then have a chance to explain the banks thinking when he testifies on the economy to a parliamentary committee on May 8.

There were few clues from a speech by deputy governor Stephen Grenville today in which he said the bank was confident it could keep inflation down through good monetary policy. He also emphasised the economy could not exceed accepted speed limits without risking inflation. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
